t: Benin City was the seat of the Ọba, whose line began, according to tradition, when a son of Ọranmiyan of Ife was set on the throne, and it grew rich in the 16th and 17th centuries on trade with Europeans in pepper and ivory.
On 17 February 1897 a British force of 1,200 men captured, sacked and burnt the city and took the bronzes from the palace, an act that opened the way to British colonisation.
The British allowed the monarchy to be restored in 1914, and after Nigeria's independence the city became the capital of the Mid-Western Region, of Bendel State and, from 1991, of Edo State.
dyk: In 1691 a Portuguese captain wrote that Great Benin was larger than Lisbon and that the people had no doors to their houses; in 1701 or 1702 a Dutch merchant called the same city a "mere village".

f.founded: According to tradition the land was first ruled by the Ogiso kings, and the present line of Ọba began when Prince Ọranmiyan of Ife sent his son to rule; Benin imperialism began in the last decade of the 13th century under Ọba Ewedo.
f.where: In southern Nigeria, the capital of Edo State, within the local government areas of Egor, Ikpoba-Okha and Oredo.
f.known: The Ọba and the kingdom of Benin; trade in pepper and ivory with the Portuguese; the city wall and moat; bronze casting and the Benin Bronzes; the British expedition of 1897
f.today: Benin City is the capital and largest city of Edo State and the fourth-largest city in Nigeria by the 2006 census.
